DNN weights and ranks

Source: vignettes/dnn-weights.Rmd
dnn-weights.Rmd

Overview

RdistNN provides two DNN rank-weight constructions:

  • method = "exact": finite-sample exact DNN coefficients
  • method = "asymp": asymptotic DNN coefficients

Use weights_dnn() to switch between them with a common interface.

The following support conventions matter in practice:

  • exact DNN weights are computed from the full rank permutation for each target, not by keeping only the first s observations;
  • for the unaveraged exact finite-population rank table, support is j <= n - s + k, and in particular j <= n - s + 1 when k = 1;
  • the asymptotic Beta-increment approximation is typically treated as a full-support rank-weight sequence.

Weights for identical localization covariate rows are averaged within each duplicate block. A block crossing the exact table’s support edge can therefore give observations beyond that rank positive weight. The block’s total mass is preserved, while individual weights and ESS can change.

Fixed top-k DNN kernels are implemented for 1 <= k <= s. The accompanying paper gives the theory for k = 1; accepting another k does not establish its inferential justification.

Basic Usage 

n <- 150
p <- 2
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
X0 <- matrix(rnorm(8), 4, p)

wt_exact <- weights_dnn(
  X = X, X0 = X0,
  distance = "l2",
  method = "exact",
  k = 1L, s = 4L,
  return = c("W", "ranks", "ord", "dx")
)

wt_asymp <- weights_dnn(
  X = X, X0 = X0,
  distance = "l2",
  method = "asymp",
  k = 1L, s = 4L,
  normalize = TRUE,
  return = "W"
)

colSums(wt_exact$W)
#> [1] 1 1 1 1
colSums(wt_asymp$W)
#> [1] 1 1 1 1

Single-target Convenience

Use x0 for one target instead of a one-row X0.

x0 <- c(0, 0)
wt_single <- weights_dnn(
  X = X, x0 = x0,
  method = "exact",
  k = 1L, s = 4L,
  return = c("W", "ranks")
)

dim(wt_single$W)  # n x 1
#> [1] 150   1

Identical covariate rows

The equality check uses every raw localization covariate exactly. Distinct vectors at equal distance remain ordered lexicographically; nearby values are not merged. For this example the original rank table is (1/2, 1/3, 1/6, 0). The two identical rows receive (1/2 + 1/3)/2 = 5/12 each:

X_tied <- matrix(c(0, 0, 1, 2), ncol = 1)
wt_tied <- weights_dnn(X = X_tied, x0 = 0, k = 1L, s = 2L)
#> Warning: Identical covariate rows detected; weights are averaged within
#> duplicate-covariate blocks, including jackknife deletions. This
#> permutation-invariant modification is not covered by the paper's theory.
drop(wt_tied$W)
#> [1] 0.4166667 0.4166667 0.1666667 0.0000000

The call warns that this permutation-invariant modification is not covered by the paper’s theory. High-level estimators apply the same policy to every delete-one sample: the deleted observation is removed before averaging the remaining block’s n-1 weights. Averaging only the full-sample weights would not define matching jackknife uncertainty. Aligned outcomes and nuisance rows must move with their covariate rows when comparing permutations.

For a block occupying ranks a:b, the full-sample weight per member is sum(w_n[a:b])/(b-a+1). Deleting a member leaves b-a survivors at ranks a:(b-1), each with weight sum(w_(n-1)[a:(b-1)])/(b-a); a deleted singleton contributes zero. The table and the denominator both change. In the example, deleting the first row raises its identical partner’s weight from 5/12 to 2/3:

wt_deleted <- weights_dnn(X = X_tied[-1L, , drop = FALSE],
                          x0 = 0, k = 1L, s = 2L)
drop(wt_deleted$W)  # 2/3, 1/3, 0
#> [1] 0.6666667 0.3333333 0.0000000

If all covariate rows are identical and weights are normalized, each receives 1/n, and each survivor receives 1/(n-1) after a deletion. Increasing s cannot distinguish identical covariates. This numerical averaging rule does not establish an inference theorem for that design.

Returned ranks and orders remain permutations used to locate the blocks. With duplicates, the final W cannot be reconstructed from a rank table alone; the grouping information is also needed. Standalone rank-only utilities have no covariates from which to infer those groups.

Working with Returned Diagnostics

return can include:

  • "W": weight matrix (n x m)
  • "ranks": rank matrix (n x m)
  • "ord": order matrix (n x m)
  • "dx": distance matrix (n x m)

These are useful when you want to:

  • verify deterministic ordering in tie settings
  • debug custom distance behavior
  • reuse ranks in downstream routines

Exact vs Asymptotic 

mu_signal <- rnorm(n)
mu_exact <- as.numeric(crossprod(mu_signal, wt_exact$W))
mu_asymp <- as.numeric(crossprod(mu_signal, wt_asymp$W))

cbind(mu_exact, mu_asymp)
#>        mu_exact   mu_asymp
#> [1,] 0.10286550 0.10246327
#> [2,] 0.11298128 0.11244305
#> [3,] 0.21969143 0.21866562
#> [4,] 0.04561642 0.04615826

Exact weights are the package default. Setting method = "asymp" changes the weight construction; it is separate from choosing a compiled or R calculation engine.

Numerical limits

Asymptotic tables use host Beta-distribution routines. At the smallest representable scales, rounding the interval endpoints can erase a tail mass or give R and Stata different zero versus nonzero support. Averaging several order statistics and combining signed TDNN tables can also lose tiny masses. This remains an unresolved numerical limitation. Extreme outcomes can make such differences visible in estimates and jackknife covariance.

Renormalizing the table or selecting a compiled deletion engine cannot recover probability already lost during table construction. Exact weights use a different finite-population rule; switching to them changes the method rather than repairing an asymptotic table. The maintainer reference on weighted accumulation describes the arithmetic and its limits.
